summary:
Onion Sky (https://onion-sky.vercel.app) is a free browser game that lets anyone search real NASA SPHEREx infrared images for moving solar-system objects. SPHEREx maps the whole sky again and again, but its data are hard to explore without astronomy software. A distant Planet X would drift only about one pixel a day across those images, so finding it takes frames spread over long stretches of time and more people looking than any one team has.

In Onion Sky, players blink between frames taken hours or days apart, colour them by time, and mark anything that moves. The server scores each answer against a hidden answer key, and a tutorial, achievements and a leaderboard keep people playing. Players can also pick any patch on an all-sky map and search it with live data. Where no answer is known, the game shows how many other players marked the same track.

Behind the game is our Python pipeline. It downloads SPHEREx images from NASA's IRSA archive, keeps each short burst of exposures separate so movers aren't smeared, and shift-and-stacks the frames (Heinze et al. 2015; Whidden et al. 2019) to reveal objects too faint for one image. It recovers the asteroids Eros and Hektor and the dwarf planets Makemake and Eris. It finds Eris blind, narrowly above a measured noise bar, and finds nothing in a control field.
details:
What it does and how it works

Our project has two parts. The first is a Python pipeline that downloads SPHEREx near-infrared images from NASA's IRSA archive (0.75 to 5 µm, 102 bands, 6.15 arcsecond pixels). It groups the exposures into short bursts, about four exposures taken two minutes apart, and treats each burst as one frame. We don't merge all 102 bands, because collecting them takes weeks of observing and anything that moves would be erased. The frames are lined up on one sky grid and shown two ways:

  • Blinking: flipping between the frames.
  • Shift-and-stack: the frames are added along a guessed motion, so a mover too faint for one frame builds up into a detection.

Each detection is compared with a noise bar, made by running the same search on sign-flipped images to see how high pure noise reaches. Known objects are also checked against JPL Horizons positions. The pipeline recovers movers ranging from fast asteroids (Eros, Hektor) to distant dwarf planets (Makemake, Eris).

The second part is Onion Sky, a web game at https://onion-sky.vercel.app. Players work with real SPHEREx fields: they blink and colour the frames, change wavelength bands and brightness, and mark a mover in at least two frames or answer "nothing moved". The server scores each answer against an answer key the browser never sees. An all-sky map lets players pick any patch of sky and play it with live IRSA data. Those patches have no answer key, so the game checks the track against known asteroids and shows how many other players marked the same one. The game also has a tutorial, achievements, a leaderboard and player accounts.

Benefits

SPHEREx data are public, but hard to use without astronomy software. The game lets anyone explore them in a browser. The pipeline gives students and researchers a documented, reproducible way to search for moving objects. We report every result with its margin, including the weak ones.

Intended impact

A distant Planet X, 400 to 800 AU from the Sun, would move only about one pixel a day, too little for a single frame to show. Finding it takes long time baselines, careful statistics and many people looking. We want to show how SPHEREx's repeated coverage of the sky can support that search, and to let the public take part, with crowd agreement as the signal where no known answer exists.

Tools and technology

  • Pipeline: Python 3.14 with NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, Astroquery, Photutils, Matplotlib, Pillow and Requests.
  • Web app: TypeScript, Next.js 16 and React 19, with Zod for input checks, Aladin Lite and HEALPix for the sky map, and Lucide icons.
  • Database: Supabase (PostgreSQL with row-level security and login) stores players, finds and the leaderboard.
  • Hosting: Vercel.
  • Data and services: NASA IRSA (SPHEREx images), JPL Horizons and the JPL small-body identification service, CDS (HiPS sky tiles, SIMBAD, Sesame) and ESA Gaia.
  • Design: the JetBrains Mono font, Orbitron font and music from Pixabay.

Creativity

The game asks players to do what astronomers do: compare images taken at different times and spot what moved. The blink controls and shift-and-stack are real analysis methods, used here as game tools. Live sky patches let anyone search parts of the sky nobody has labelled. There, agreement between players takes the place of the missing answer key.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty:
    • Every detection comes with a noise bar.
    • "Nothing moved" counts as a correct answer.
    • We use motion rates measured on SPHEREx data. SPHEREx looks roughly sideways from the Sun, so the usual formula for objects opposite the Sun gives the wrong rates.
    • Points are calculated only on the server.
    • Answer keys never reach the browser.
    • Agreement counts each player once.
    • Colour-blind-safe time colours (Okabe-Ito).
    • Flashing capped at three frames per second.
    • Support for reduced motion.
    • Keyboard controls and screen-reader labels.
    • SPHEREx and IRSA data are credited.
    • Every font, sound and package was checked.
    • The code is open source under GPL-3.0.
